findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Clarify whether the ancestor-descendant rejection is signalled as `is_redundant: True` or `{"error": ...}` in the resolver's return dict, and update the `_hierarchy.py` scope bullet and AC3 to use the same term consistently.
evidence: Scope/_hierarchy.py: 'widen `is_redundant` from direct parent-child to any ancestor-descendant pair'
Scope/composer.py: 'once the resolver returns `{"error": ...}` for an ancestor pair'
AC3: '`resolve_hierarchy_link` returns an error for any blocking pair where one endpoint is an ancestor of the other'
findings.finding: The `_hierarchy.py` scope bullet says 'widen `is_redundant` from direct parent-child to any ancestor-descendant pair', but the `composer.py` scope and AC3 treat the ancestor-descendant case as returning a distinct `{"error": ...}` key — not `is_redundant: true`. An executor faces a genuine design fork: does detecting that one endpoint is an ancestor of the other produce `is_redundant=True` in the resolver's return dict, or does it produce a separate `error` key? The two representations require different handling in both `_links.py` and `composer.py`.
findings.location: Scope section — `src/rebar/graph/_hierarchy.py` bullet ('widen `is_redundant`…') vs. `src/rebar/_commands/composer.py` bullet ('Add a branch on `res.get("error")`…') and AC3
scenarios: Executor implements ancestor-descendant as is_redundant=True, but composer.py expects res.get('error') — the dry-run branch added in composer.py never fires.
Executor implements it as error key, but _links.py's existing is_redundant guard (which the scope says to re-evaluate on the resolved pair) is bypassed.
findings.suggested_fix: State explicitly: 'when escalation would produce a link where one resolved endpoint is an ancestor of the other, `resolve_hierarchy_link` returns `{"error": "ancestor-descendant", "source": …, "target": …}` (not `is_redundant`); `is_redundant` continues to flag only the case where the resolved link duplicates an already-recorded edge.' Update the `_hierarchy.py` scope bullet to remove the 'widen is_redundant' phrasing for this case.

evidence: Scope _hierarchy.py: 'widen `is_redundant` from direct parent-child to any ancestor-descendant pair'
Scope composer.py: 'Add a branch on `res.get("error")` before the existing `is_redundant` branch'
AC3: '`resolve_hierarchy_link` returns an error for any blocking pair where one endpoint is an ancestor of the other'
findings.finding: Scope for `_hierarchy.py` says 'widen `is_redundant` from direct parent-child to any ancestor-descendant pair', implying the resolver emits `is_redundant: true` for the ancestor case. But Scope for `composer.py` says to add a branch on `res.get("error")` BEFORE the `is_redundant` branch, and AC3 says the resolver 'returns an error' for the ancestor pair. These are two different response-key shapes for the same scenario; an implementer cannot satisfy both simultaneously.
findings.location: Scope (`src/rebar/graph/_hierarchy.py` bullet, last sentence) vs Scope (`src/rebar/_commands/composer.py` bullet) vs AC3
scenarios: Implementer widens is_redundant → composer.py `res.get("error")` branch never fires, dry-run falls through to 'Would create' for a link the real path rejects (the exact bug the composer change is meant to fix).
Implementer uses `error` key → `is_redundant` widen never happens, but Scope line says it should.
findings.suggested_fix: Pick `{"error": "ancestor-descendant"}` (matching the composer.py and AC3 language) and change the `_hierarchy.py` scope bullet to 'return an error dict for any ancestor-descendant blocking pair' rather than widening `is_redundant`.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Correct the deletion-safety rationale in the Approach section: the four symbols are safe to remove because `grep -rn` finds no references outside `_hierarchy.py` (the grep evidence), NOT because `__all__` exports only two symbols — `__init__.py`'s `__all__` actually includes `_hierarchy` as a submodule export and many other symbols beyond `resolve_hierarchy_link` and `compute_archive_eligible`.
evidence: Plan quote: 'the package `__all__` (`src/rebar/graph/__init__.py:28`) re-exports only `resolve_hierarchy_link` and `compute_archive_eligible` from this module, so none of the four is part of the package surface'
`src/rebar/graph/__init__.py` lines 28-44: `__all__` contains `'_hierarchy'` as a submodule export alongside many other symbols beyond the two named ones

Direct reading: `__all__ = ['build_dep_graph', 'check_cycle_at_level', 'check_would_create_cycle', 'resolve_hierarchy_link', 'compute_archive_eligible', 'CyclicDependencyError', 'add_dependency', 'reduce_ticket', '_is_active_link', '_find_direct_blockers', '_compute_dep_graph', '_blockers', '_cache', '_graph', '_hierarchy', '_links']`
findings.finding: The plan asserts 'the package `__all__` (`src/rebar/graph/__init__.py:28`) re-exports **only** `resolve_hierarchy_link` and `compute_archive_eligible` from this module' as the safety basis for concluding the four deleted symbols are not part of the package surface. Reading `__init__.py` lines 28-44 shows `__all__` also includes `'_hierarchy'` (the submodule object itself). Because `_hierarchy` is exported as an attribute of `rebar.graph`, any caller doing `rebar.graph._hierarchy._TYPE_TIER` (or equivalent) could access the deleted symbols via the submodule reference. The deletion-safety claim rests on the stronger (and false) premise that only the two named symbols are exported; the actual guarantee is only that the four names are not directly listed in `__all__`.
findings.location: Approach section — 'Removal is safe because … the package `__all__` (`src/rebar/graph/__init__.py:28`) re-exports only `resolve_hierarchy_link` and `compute_archive_eligible` from this module'
scenarios: A caller using `rebar.graph._hierarchy._TYPE_TIER` or `rebar.graph._hierarchy._promote_to_tier` directly (e.g. a test or script patching the submodule) would break silently after deletion — the plan's safety argument does not account for this access path.

The grep-based AC ('grep -rn for each of the four names across src/ and tests/ returning no matches') would catch this if such callers exist, but the plan's stated rationale is factually incorrect and could mislead reviewers.
findings.suggested_fix: Replace 'the package `__all__` re-exports only `resolve_hierarchy_link` and `compute_archive_eligible` from this module, so none of the four is part of the package surface' with: 'none of the four names appears in `__all__` directly, and `grep -rn` across `src/` and `tests/` (excluding `_hierarchy.py` itself) returns no matches — the grep evidence alone establishes deletion safety.'

findings.finding: The plan's deletion-safety justification for `_TYPE_TIER` and the tier helpers incorrectly characterises `src/rebar/graph/__init__.py`'s `__all__`. The plan states it 'exports only `resolve_hierarchy_link` and `compute_archive_eligible` from this module'; in reality `__all__` (which starts at line 28, not 27) also includes the `_hierarchy` submodule itself (`"_hierarchy"` at line 45), making `rebar.graph._hierarchy._TYPE_TIER` technically accessible to any importer. A grep confirms no caller currently exploits this path, so deletion is safe in practice, but the stated justification is factually wrong and could cause a code reviewer to accept an incorrect premise.
findings.location: Approach section — 'They are safe to remove because … not re-exported from src/rebar/graph/__init__.py, whose __all__ (src/rebar/graph/__init__.py:27) exports only resolve_hierarchy_link and compute_archive_eligible from this module'
findings.suggested_fix: Replace: '…not re-exported from src/rebar/graph/__init__.py, whose __all__ (src/rebar/graph/__init__.py:27) exports only resolve_hierarchy_link and compute_archive_eligible from this module.' With: '…not referenced by any caller outside _hierarchy.py: a grep of src/ and tests/ for _TYPE_TIER, _tier_of, _tier_of_ticket, and _promote_to_tier returns only definitions within _hierarchy.py itself. Although src/rebar/graph/__init__.py's __all__ includes the _hierarchy submodule (line 45), no code accesses the tier helpers through that path.'

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Clarify whether the `is_redundant` ancestor-descendant widening is scoped to blocking relations only, and if so, ensure the resolver either gates the widened check on `relation in _BLOCKING_RELATIONS` before setting `is_redundant`, or that `add_dependency` gates its `is_redundant` rejection on blocking relations — and add a test asserting that `relates_to` on a direct parent-child pair still succeeds.
evidence: Plan Scope: 'widen `is_redundant` from direct parent-child to any ancestor-descendant pair' — no relation-scoping qualifier
hierarchy.py:163-167: is_redundant computed before relation branch, returned for non-blocking path at line 175
links.py:180: `if hierarchy_result.get('is_redundant')` — not gated on relation

Plan Approach: 'The non-blocking early return at src/rebar/graph/_hierarchy.py:170 ... are unchanged: relates_to / duplicates / supersedes / discovered_from / caused_by still record the exact pair' — implies non-blocking on parent-child pairs should still be allowed, contradicting an unscoped is_redundant widening
findings.finding: The plan says 'widen is_redundant from direct parent-child to any ancestor-descendant pair' (Scope section) but does not specify whether this widening applies only to blocking relations or to all relations. The flag is currently set before the relation-branch split (hierarchy.py:163-167) and is returned in both the non-blocking path (line 175) and the blocking path (line 227). add_dependency (links.py:180) checks is_redundant regardless of relation. If the widened check runs for non-blocking relations, relates_to / duplicates / supersedes on a parent→child pair — which the current code permits — would suddenly be rejected with a 'parent-child relationship' ValueError, a silent breaking change not called out in the plan. If the widened check should be relation-scoped (blocking only), the plan must say so and the implementation must scope it accordingly.
findings.location: Scope section — '`src/rebar/graph/_hierarchy.py` — widen `is_redundant` from direct parent-child to any ancestor-descendant pair'; also `src/rebar/graph/_links.py:180`
scenarios: A user links `relates_to` between a story and its own task child — currently allowed, but would be rejected if is_redundant is widened without scoping.
The resolver returns is_redundant=True for a non-blocking parent-child pair under the new ancestor-descendant definition, add_dependency raises ValueError, breaking existing callers.
findings.suggested_fix: In the new resolver, compute the ancestor-descendant `is_redundant` (or `is_ancestor_descendant`) flag only within the blocking-relations branch, returning `False` (or omitting the field) for non-blocking relations. Alternatively, rename the field to `is_ancestor_descendant` and gate the rejection in `add_dependency` on `relation in _BLOCKING_RELATIONS`.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Add an explicit rollback/back-out plan (e.g., a feature flag, a revert commit tag, or an expand-contract sequence) for the resolver behavior change so that unexpected production rejections from the new structural rule can be reversed without a full redeploy cycle.
evidence: Plan says: 'it breaks existing callers that rely on auto-escalation — the link MCP tool and the reconciler's inbound apply path … under a fail-open except Exception'
Plan says reconciler is fail-open but does not describe what happens when the MCP tool receives the new {"error":…} shape for a previously-succeeding ancestor-descendant link
No section in the plan describes how to revert if the new semantics cause unexpected production rejections
Criterion T4 states: 'The remedy is an explicit rollback/back-out plan or expand-contract — acknowledgement alone is insufficient'
findings.finding: The plan changes resolver behavior (structural NCA rule replaces type-tier rule, ancestor-descendant pairs now rejected rather than silently mis-promoted) in a way that affects at least two live callers — the `link` MCP tool and the reconciler's apply path — but provides no rollback or back-out plan. The criterion requires an explicit reversibility mechanism, not just acknowledgement of the break.
findings.location: Approach section (caller discussion) and Out of scope section; no rollback section exists anywhere in the plan.
scenarios: A caller that previously passed an ancestor-descendant pair and received a (wrong but non-crashing) escalated edge now receives an error; if the MCP tool surfaces that error unexpectedly, operators need to revert — but no revert path is described.

If the NCA traversal has an edge case not covered by tests (e.g., a ticket with a parent in a partially-loaded store), the new rejection behavior could block linking entirely with no way to temporarily fall back to the old rule.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a short 'Rollback' section: identify the single commit (or PR) that swaps the resolver branch, note that reverting it restores type-tier behavior for new links (existing store data is unaffected either way), and confirm the sibling audit ticket 9ad7 must not run until this ticket is stable — giving a clear sequenced back-out path.

findings.finding: The reconciler's `apply_inbound_records.py:502` calls `rebar.link` under a `fail-open except Exception`. After this change, `add_dependency` raises `ValueError` for ancestor-descendant pairs. If a reconciled inbound record resolves to an ancestor-descendant pair under the new NCA rule, the `except Exception` silently swallows the rejection — no error is surfaced to the operator, the record is not retried, and the bad link is silently dropped. The plan notes the caller exists but does not address whether the new error class propagates or is swallowed.

findings.suggested_fix: In the Scope section, add a bullet: `src/rebar/_engine/rebar_reconciler/apply_inbound_records.py` — within the `except Exception` block at line 502, add a structured log entry (e.g., `logger.warning("link rejected: %s", exc)`) before the fail-open continue, so ancestor-descendant rejections from the new rule are surfaced in reconciler output.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Explicitly enumerate in the Scope section the three existing test functions whose assertions invert under the structural rule (`test_add_dependency_cross_story_redirects_to_story_level`, `test_add_dependency_cross_story_emits_redirect_json_to_stdout`, `test_resolve_hierarchy_link_cross_story_same_epic_sc3`) and describe their new expected values, so implementers know to update them rather than just add new cases.
evidence: test_add_dependency_cross_story_redirects_to_story_level (adddep:26-82): asserts task-a1 promotes to epic-root when linking to unrelated epic-other. Under structural rule these are disjoint trees (no common ancestor) so escalation does NOT happen — assertion inverts.

test_add_dependency_cross_story_emits_redirect_json_to_stdout (adddep:108-155): asserts redirected=True and resolved.source=epic-root2 for task-x1→epic-target (disjoint trees). Under structural rule: no redirect, assertion inverts.

test_resolve_hierarchy_link_cross_story_same_epic_sc3 (resolve:61-102): asserts was_redirected=False for task-a1 (under story-a) → task-b1 (under story-b), both under epic-root. Under structural rule, NCA is epic-root; both escalate to story-a and story-b — was_redirected=True, assertion inverts.
Plan scope text: 'existing type-tier expectations are updated to the structural rule' — no specific test IDs named.
findings.finding: Three existing tests in the named test files have assertions that directly encode the old type-tier rule and will fully invert under the new structural rule — not 'update' but reverse. The plan says only 'existing type-tier expectations are updated' without naming them, leaving an implementer unaware that test_add_dependency_cross_story_redirects_to_story_level, test_add_dependency_cross_story_emits_redirect_json_to_stdout, and test_resolve_hierarchy_link_cross_story_same_epic_sc3 will fail in the opposite direction.
findings.location: Scope / tests/scripts/graph/test_graph_hierarchy_adddep.py and test_graph_hierarchy_resolve.py
scenarios: Developer adds new tests (as the plan requires), all new tests pass, but three existing tests fail because their expected values were not updated.
CI red on existing tests blocks merge even though the new behaviour is correct.
findings.suggested_fix: In the Scope bullet for each test file, add a sub-list of existing test cases whose assertions change, with the new expected value, e.g. 'test_add_dependency_cross_story_redirects_to_story_level: update to assert was_redirected=False and LINK written in task-a1 dir (disjoint trees, no NCA → no escalation)'. Similarly for the SC3 test.
